newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone junta hardens position at talks.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone junta hardens position at talks.

text.p: Sierra Leone's army junta has hardened its position at talks in which West African foreign ministers are trying to reverse the May 25 coup in Freetown, conference sources said on Wednesday.
Nigeria is leading pressure by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to evict the army from power in the same way the junta in Haiti was forced out in 1993.
But after agreeing in principle to restore democracy the Freetown junta is now demanding recognition from ECOWAS, among other conditions, the sources said at the talks in Ivory Coast.
"We are talking about an entrenched regime being asked to stand down. It has never happened in Africa and it won't be easy in the case of Sierra Leone," a diplomat told Reuters.
Junta delegates have argued that, by holding talks with them, the 16-member ECOWAS had implicitly recognised their government. They want a transitional period to restoreV democracy.
The ministers insist on the immediate restoration of the deposed government of elected president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

The return of Kabbah, who is exiled in neighbouring Guinea, is a key demand of the Organisation of African Unity. It is also a central part of an agreement signed by both sides at an earlier meeting on July 18, ECOWAS officials say.
Conference sources said they did not see how that sticking point would be resolved given Nigeria's uncompromising insistence on Kabbah's return to power.

Diplomats comparing the crisis in Sierra Leone with that of Haiti in 1991-93, said ECOWAS could not conceivably return Kabbah to power without a credible threat of the use of force against the junta -- the way the United States did in Haiti.

Soldiers toppled Haiti's elected president Jean Betrand Aristide in October 1991, forcing him to flee to Venezuela. Aristide was returned to power two years later to serve out his term with the backing of U.S. and other regional troops.
The Sierra Leone coup was condemned worldwide, with the international community demanding the restoration of Kabbah.

Nigerian troops leading a regional military force, ECOMOG, bombarded Freetown on June 2 trying to reverse the coup. The poorly coordinated attack failed and Nigeria has since joined regional efforts to negotiate the departure of the junta.

"There doesn't appear to be any country in ECOWAS prepared to join Nigeria in using force in Sierra Leone," a diplomat at the talks said. "And it doesn't look like Nigerians will want to go it alone after their experience on June 2."
The latest talks in Abidjan opened on Tuesday but quickly became bogged down over the detention of Sierra Leone rebel leader Foday Sankoh in Nigeria.
The ministers from regional power Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea and Ivory Coast, had expected fast progress following agreement on restoring democracy at the earlier meeting.
But the Freetown team unexpectedly demanded that Sankoh, whose rebels rallied to the coup, join them at the meeting.
Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front waged a five-year bush war in Sierra Leone from 1991 before signing an accord in November 1996 with Kabbah.

Delegates said the two sides did not appear to have reached a common ground despite intensive lobbying through the night. A scheduled resumption of the full session was put back by five hours from 9.00 A.M. (0900 GMT).
Junior officers toppled Kabbah, accusing him of violating the accord with Sankoh. RUF guerrillas rallied to the coup and entered the capital in their thousands.
Sankoh, who was in Nigeria at the time, was detained in prison after he his men to join the coup soldiers.
The junta agreed to restore civilian rule but maintains Kabbah cannot return as president. It wants an end to a crippling economic embargo imposed by ECOWAS since the coup.
